title: I shipped my first iOS game with AI doing the code, art and audio – here's what actually worked (and what didn't)
author: Good_Active_2261
selftext:
Moon Quack! just went live on the App Store: a one-thumb arcade game where every tap fires a duck's jetpack, but every boost burns fuel, so you're constantly trading altitude for fuel while dodging missiles and lasers on the way to the Moon. Built in Unity, with AI involved in almost every part of the pipeline – a few things I learned along the way:

\*\*Code (Claude as a coding assistant).\*\* The whole Unity project was written together with Claude. What made the biggest difference wasn't code generation itself but using it to build tools: headless "human-like" bots with different skill levels that play every level, so I could tune difficulty, fuel and the coin economy against a target win-rate table instead of guessing. Without that, balancing a long level curve as a solo dev would have been impossible.

\*\*Art (Leonardo AI).\*\* Characters, backgrounds and props are Leonardo, mostly Phoenix with an illustration style. Keeping the duck consistent was the hard part – prompt-only character references kept breaking him (white ducks, human arms). What worked was taking one good image and making single, targeted edits with the "add or remove things" editor. Chaining edits slowly destroys the image, so I always went back to the last good version. Another trick: if the prompt describes the duck, Leonardo puts a duck in every prop, so object prompts had to say "inanimate object only" with "duck, character" in the negatives. Flames and effects are drawn in code, not baked into the art.

\*\*Audio (ElevenLabs).\*\* All sound effects plus a music loop per world. Mid-energy (\~108 bpm) worked best; the "calm" versions turned into sleep music.

Happy to answer questions about any part of the workflow. Free on iPhone & iPad: [https://apps.apple.com/app/id6826553955](https://apps.apple.com/app/id6826553955)
